text:
She said his name wrong. Three times.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> didn't correct her. The apartment smelled like camphor and fear-sweat and something frying in old oil three doors down. He'd been standing in it for twenty minutes — long enough to stop noticing the smell and start belonging to it. Her husband sat in the corner with his jaw wired shut, breathing slow through his nose. The jaw no longer got a vote.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> took a step toward the corner, toward the husband, to see the shape of what had been done. <entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-3404-79c2-a8f6-2942f504698e">The woman</entity> moved. She put herself between them, back straight, the payment already out in her hand. "This part's done." <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> stopped.

She pressed the credstick into his palm. Warm chip, a little damp. He didn't check the balance while she watched. Reading it in front of her would be its own small theft.

He looked at it in the hall.

Φ180. Half his usual rate, for a job that had cost him three hours and his left shoulder. His shoulder chose that moment to remind him what the three hours had cost it, and he let the wince go through his jaw and nowhere else. He stood there with the stick in his palm and didn't make a thing of the number. He thought about how she'd gripped it before she handed it over - the grip of someone who'd been carrying it in her fist long before she made the call.

He pocketed it and took the stairs down.

The katana rode across his back in a plain matte-black sheath. Carbon-nanotube composite, no markings, nothing that could earn a name. <entity repo="weapon" guid="4ab24f74-61d4-4f45-b326-7c6b98c96279">Cacophony</entity> rode low on his left hip - six rounds in <entity repo="weapon" guid="4ab24f74-61d4-4f45-b326-7c6b98c96279">the cylinder</entity>, hammer resting, the way it always rested. He walked out of the building and into the <entity repo="place" guid="019d6143-a927-73ac-abfa-37c77f9cff8d">GLMZ</entity> night like a man who'd done nothing worth remembering. That was the point. It took effort.

He'd taken the job at half rate and told himself it was because of the jaw.

The jaw, wired shut. A man cut down to breathing and waiting. The woman had gripped the credstick like it was the last thing she'd ever own, which meant it probably was, and she'd known what half rate bought her—no guarantees, no second visit, a man who'd walk out the door and not come back if the door turned out to be worse than she'd said. He'd taken it anyway. Because the alternative was explaining why the husband's jaw was the price of full rates, and some explanations cost more than money.

The math was simple. The math was always simple. Half rate meant half a reason, and half a reason was all a broken man could afford to give himself.

What he didn't let himself count was the girl.

Not the woman. The girl. Behind the curtain in the hallway, maybe sixteen, maybe younger—the age where the metrics stopped keeping track. The woman hadn't mentioned a daughter. The girl hadn't made a sound. She'd just been there in the gap where the curtain didn't quite meet the frame, elbows on her knees, watching him the way children watch a thing they've already decided to remember.

Not threat-assessment. Not curiosity. He knew the difference; reading a room was the first thing they beat into you. This was neither. This was recognition, and it followed him across the small apartment with the specific weight of attention that has a shape—watching him take the credstick, watching the way he carried the shoulder, watching a man who'd accepted half-rate work and walked out like it was a choice he'd made with his whole body.

Like she was seeing something she already knew was coming.

He didn't slow. Slowing was how you became a landmark, and landmarks got noticed twice.

He told himself the girl was someone else's problem, someone else's future, someone else's reason to be afraid of what she'd seen.

He almost believed it.

title: Chapter 1 — Teeth
text:
<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> felt the frequency before he saw it. A low hum in the 17-to-19 hertz band — a schism, the kind of tear in the world the city had learned to route around, the absence that registered in his teeth before it registered anywhere else. Four seconds later his eyes found the proof: a cigarette pack, two pebbles, a length of wire, and what might have been the clip off a lanyard, all turning in a slow circle around one fixed spot in the turn lane at 14th and Blue Island.

The circle was slow. The pebbles moved against the wind.

He measured how wide it ran and took Racine instead. Nothing dramatic — Racine was fine, and the extra three minutes still put him at the site on time. The schism might be gone in half an hour or it might last three days. There was no way to know without a tracking team, and nobody was going to send a tracking team for a cigarette pack circling a crack in the asphalt at 14th and Blue Island. The morning's Schism Advisory for Zone 4 had listed two active ones. He had been expecting this one. The Advisory never listed all of them — it listed the ones somebody had walked out and stood next to long enough to log, which meant it listed the ones near the truce counters and the corpo frontages and none of the ones out here, where the Substrate coverage overhead was already a stuttering ghost of itself and the buildings had learned to stop looking.

He kept going.

And then the hum found him again — the same 17-to-19 band, dead ahead, where Racine bent toward the site. This one he saw before he'd finished measuring the first: a hubcap, a fan of wet newspaper, a child's shoe, all wheeling around a fixed point that sat squarely across both lanes. Not routed around. Routing itself, closing the gap he'd chosen. The Advisory had listed two. This was a third, and it was moving to meet him.

He killed the engine and checked the band again, and the number had climbed — 21 hertz now, the range where the tracking teams stopped talking about detours and started talking about teeth. He knew that number the way a musician knows a note that's just slightly wrong. Behind him, in the mirror, the cigarette pack at Blue Island had stopped circling. It hung in the air, pointed his way, like something that had decided.

There was no clean road to the site anymore, and he was already late for the only thing that mattered.

He parked the bike a block out and walked the rest. The crew on the loading dock wouldn't be expecting him. Surprise was free.

The dock sat at the bottom of the eastern strut, where the architecture stopped pretending to be architecture and became what it was — welded industrial grief. The afternoon light came in flat and grey, the kind that made every surface look like it was made of ash. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> moved through it without hurrying. Hurrying would have been a tell.

He came in the front. The personnel door beside the roll-up had a steel pull handle worn mirror-bright in one long oval, the exact shape of ten thousand hands closing on it in the same place while the rest of the door went on rusting around it. No hood. No sideways angle in. He wanted the moment — the exact moment when six people who'd spent weeks feeling like a force of nature looked up and saw the weather walk in the door.

He hauled the door open and stepped into the light, and the dock was empty.

Not the kind of empty where people had just stepped away. The kind where nobody had been there in hours, and somebody had wanted it to look that way. The concrete was clean — swept, actually swept, which meant someone had thought about what the space would look like on a screen. Six pallets stood where six people should have been, and on the nearest one someone had left a phone propped against a crate, screen bright, angled to catch exactly the spot he stood in now.

The indicator light was red.

It was recording. It had been recording before he arrived. He knew that the way you know a room is wrong the second you're in it — the phone hadn't turned itself on for him, hadn't tracked him, hadn't done anything but hold a fixed frame and wait for him to walk into it. He looked at the lens and the screen showed him back to himself: shoulders, the dark line of <entity repo="weapon" guid="4ab24f74-61d4-4f45-b326-7c6b98c96279">Cacophony</entity>'s grip near his hand, his face rendered in the phone's cheap color grading as something between ash and copper. Holding still. Patient. Documented.

They hadn't been surprised. They'd been waiting — somewhere else, watching him walk into a room built to receive him. He didn't touch the phone. Above him the sky had gone the color of old copper, the atmospheric processors working overtime, pushing something or pulling something the way they did when the city was nervous, and <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> stood in the frame they'd left for him and understood, finally, that he was no longer the one holding the knife.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> stepped across the line that separates the weather from the room, and stood still, and let them look.

One of them had a chrome arm — a full replacement, the shoulder-socket kind, packed with myomer and hydraulics, strong enough to punch through light vehicle plating. Across the table sat a woman his array flagged before <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>'s eyes found the reason: slight, still, her weight already on the balls of her feet, hardware nested at every hinge of her. Actuator housings at the wrists, the elbows, the knees, the toes of her boots. Retractable blades. Someone had rebuilt her joint by joint into a knife block — a Splicer with skill, working for a buyer with intent, nothing about it for show. A third man had sub-dermal plating under his skin, the seams showing at his collar like a man wearing himself wrong. A fourth had a jaw modification done badly enough to pull the skin tight down the left side of his face — cheap and fast, a man who'd had his face broken before and hadn't kept the original parts. The fifth was younger, chrome only at the knuckles: discharge plates, the kind that threw sparks on contact and let a twenty-year-old hit like a forklift, as long as whatever he hit agreed to hold still. He was already rolling his shoulder. The sixth had no augmentation <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> could see. Which meant it was inside him, where it was expensive. The man who'd paid for expensive and invisible was the one giving the orders. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> tracked him first.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>'s eyes found the jaw man last — the bad work, the wired mouth. His hand dropped to <entity repo="weapon" guid="4ab24f74-61d4-4f45-b326-7c6b98c96279">Cacophony</entity>. Six bodies, already sorted. The chrome-arm man was out of his chair before <entity repo="weapon" guid="4ab24f74-61d4-4f45-b326-7c6b98c96279">the cylinder</entity> cleared the holster: one step, the chrome hand closing around <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>'s wrist. Not a grab — a commitment. Not squeezing. Just there, pressure with a specific number behind it, enough to hold and not enough to break, the kind of grip that didn't care about pain thresholds or surrender. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> let the grip go.

The chrome hand didn't squeeze. That was the tell.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> let the grip go—not releasing <entity repo="weapon" guid="4ab24f74-61d4-4f45-b326-7c6b98c96279">Cacophony</entity>, just allowing the wrist to go slack, the revolver still in his palm but pointed at the floor. The man with the expensive invisible augmentation had already stopped moving. The younger one with the discharge plates kept his shoulder roll going, a tell of his own: nerves, or theater.

"Renner's not here," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> said.

The chrome-arm man released him. Stepped back one pace. Not a retreat. A reset.

"Not yet," the sixth man said. His voice was quiet—the kind of quiet that comes from someone who doesn't need to raise volume to be heard. "He's running late. But you already knew that."

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> had not known that. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>'s array had flagged the room the moment he entered: six augmented operatives, a card table with cash and chips scattered mid-hand, the overhead light casting sharp shadows that meant no surveillance, no audio feed, no relay connection. The room was clean in the way that required planning and access. The room was a stage.

"He sent word you'd be coming," the sixth man continued. He gestured to an empty chair at the table—the only empty chair, positioned so <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>'s back would be to the door he'd used. "Wanted you to sit. Wanted to know if you'd fold."

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> didn't move.

"You fold early," the man said. "You fold clean. You don't ask questions about the game before you decide." He leaned back in his chair, and the motion was casual enough that it almost landed as genuine. "Renner thinks that means you're scared. I think it means you're smart. Wanted to verify which one."

The woman with <entity repo="weapon" guid="cd8ce222-de5f-44c4-b6f6-5c18721c1050">the blade</entity>-work didn't blink. The chrome-arm man was already back in his chair, one hand resting on the table edge where <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> could see it. The jaw man with the wired mouth had his attention fixed on the chip stack in front of him—the only person in the room not watching <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>, which meant he was the only person in the room <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> needed to watch.

"I'm not here to play cards," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> said.

"No," the sixth man agreed. "You're here because Renner called in a marker. And Renner's markers tend to come due when someone needs to know whether a man can sit still in a room full of teeth without his augmentations making him a cheat." He picked up a card from the deck in front of him—a single card, casual, the way you might do if you were thinking through a problem. "Question is: can you."

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>'s hand was still on <entity repo="weapon" guid="4ab24f74-61d4-4f45-b326-7c6b98c96279">Cacophony</entity>. His array was still cataloging threat vectors. The chrome-arm man had myomer response time of approximately 0.3 seconds per joint. The blade-work woman was faster—probably 0.15, given the quality of the installation. The jaw man was the wild variable. No visible augmentation meant he was either baseline or military-grade, and military-grade operatives didn't usually take card-game work.

"What's the marker," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> said.

"Sit down," the sixth man said. "We'll tell you when the hand's finished."

---

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> sat.

The chrome-arm man dealt. Five cards, facedown, one at a time, the motion smooth and practiced. The blade-work woman checked her cards without lifting them from the table. The jaw man picked his up, looked once, and set them down again. The sixth man took his time—examining each card as it landed, as if the act of receiving five pieces of cardboard required deliberation.

The younger one with the discharge plates folded immediately. The chrome-arm man bet aggressive, the way he'd been betting aggressive on weak hands all night—<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> had watched three hands of it from the doorway, long enough to learn the shape of the table before he was part of it. The ante was Φ20. The blade-work woman called. The jaw man raised, and when he did, his wired mouth pulled tight—not a smile, just the mechanical consequence of the actuators under his skin tightening against the wire.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> watched the sixth man's eyes. They didn't move to his cards. They stayed on the jaw man. And stayed there through the raise, through the chrome-arm man's call, through <entity repo="weapon" guid="cd8ce222-de5f-44c4-b6f6-5c18721c1050">the blade</entity>-work woman's raise-back, the sequence accelerating now, chips pushed to the center in the particular way that meant real money—not the play kind, the kind that kept rent paid or didn't—the stakes climbing past casual money into the territory where people started to sweat.

"What's the marker," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> said again.

"After the hand," the sixth man said. But his eyes had shifted now—they were on <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> instead of the jaw man. Measuring something. "Question's still the same. Can you sit still?"

The younger one with the discharge plates was watching too. All of them were, except <entity repo="weapon" guid="cd8ce222-de5f-44c4-b6f6-5c18721c1050">the blade</entity>-work woman, who was still studying her cards like they might rearrange themselves if she concentrated hard enough.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>'s array was running hot. Threat assessment climbing. The room had gone quiet except for the sound of chips being pushed across the table, the soft percussion of money deciding its own fate.

"Renner's not coming," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> said.

The sixth man smiled. It was a small smile—the kind that doesn't reach the eyes. "No. Renner's not. But someone is."

Behind <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>, the door opened.

Cold air came through first—the kind of cold that means the hallway has been empty for a while, the kind that means someone's been standing in it, waiting. Then footsteps. Deliberate. Not rushing, not cautious, just *there*, the way you walk when you already know everyone in the room and none of them can touch you.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> didn't turn around.

"Deal me in," a woman's voice said. It was a voice <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> had heard before—in a stairwell, in the rain, in a moment that had cost him everything he thought he was. "I want to know if he folds."

The jaw man pushed his cards away from the table. Stood up, the motion smooth and practiced, and walked to the wall by the door and leaned there, not looking back. The chrome-arm man didn't move. The blade-work woman kept her eyes on her cards—which meant she'd already calculated seventeen responses and was waiting to see which one <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> would make first.

The sixth man gestured to the empty chair. The woman in the brown coat sat down.

She had a gun in her right hand. Compact, matte, hammer down—the kind of thing that lived in a waistband and didn't announce itself until it had already made its point. She set it on the table next to the chip stack—not threatening, just *there*, the way you might set down a cigarette or a glass of water. The motion was casual enough that it took <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>'s array two full seconds to register what he was seeing.

Two more seconds before his body understood what it meant.

She wasn't here to fold.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>'s chest warmed — the array coming up from idle into the sharpness it saved for rooms like this. A deep heat behind the sternum, cellular, like a coal blown back to life.

The room came into focus. Six bodies. <entity repo="vocabulary" guid="019d6143-aab8-7e48-97ef-8183dc295aba">Heat</entity> coming off each of them. The capacitor whine of the knuckle plates waking at the card table. The double click of the woman's wrist housings unlocking under her sleeves, quiet as a watch being wound. The boy's shoulder giving away its swing before the swing had finished forming in him.

The NeoCortex called it ballistic precognition. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> thought that was the wrong word. The array didn't predict anything. It caught the half-second that was already in motion and showed it to him plainly, and his body was moving before he'd finished the thought.

It showed him one more thing, and this it drew brighter than all the rest: the arteries. Every major line in the room, laid over the bodies in light — the sixth man's carotid running jaw to collarbone, the chrome-arm man's femoral a bright thread down the inside of his thigh, <entity repo="weapon" guid="cd8ce222-de5f-44c4-b6f6-5c18721c1050">the blade</entity>-work woman's radials threading her forearms. The plumbing that kept these men alive. Chrome was fair game. The bright lines were not. <entity repo="vocabulary" guid="019d6143-aa9b-75e1-9656-810a0ad5cd5d">Cut</entity> everything; cross nothing. That was the whole of his code, and the array held the map so his hand could keep to it.

Then the map stuttered. For a quarter-second the bright lines guttered and doubled, ghosting sideways off the bodies — six arteries becoming twelve, the true ones and the false ones overlaid and indistinguishable. A carotid became two carotids became four, each one equally vivid, equally present, each a path to death depending on which one was actually there. The chrome-arm man's femoral flickered between two locations, one real, one phantom, both bright as fresh blood. The heat behind his sternum spiked past sharpness into something that burned, and a hairline of static crawled across his vision like a cracked lens. He knew that feeling. He'd felt it once before, in a clinic in Sao Paulo, right before a tech had told him the array was drawing more from his nervous system than it was ever meant to, and that one day it would ask for everything at once.

The boy's shoulder finished its swing. And <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>, for the first time in this line of work, could not tell which of the two lines laid over the man's throat was the one he had to spare.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>'s left hand found the saya. The motion was automatic — muscle memory written into the neural lattice over a decade of repetition, the kind of thing the array could execute without asking permission from the conscious mind.

His right hand was already moving. He cleared the saya in one unbroken draw — right hand over the right shoulder, <entity repo="weapon" guid="cd8ce222-de5f-44c4-b6f6-5c18721c1050">the blade</entity> sliding free of the composite friction saya with a sound like cloth tearing, the whisper of carbon-nanotube against composite lining, so quiet it was almost not there. Almost. <entity repo="weapon" guid="019ed39c-6321-7c51-9691-f59b441b0bec">Silence</entity> was alive in the air at the bottom of the motion, the draw silent and complete in the time it took the boy's shoulder to finish its arc. No flourish. The spine of <entity repo="weapon" guid="cd8ce222-de5f-44c4-b6f6-5c18721c1050">the blade</entity> was matte black and stayed matte black; the dock's amber overheads found nothing on it to catch, because catching light was not what <entity repo="weapon" guid="cd8ce222-de5f-44c4-b6f6-5c18721c1050">the blade</entity> was for.

The man blocking the stairwell had not moved yet, but he would, and when he did <entity repo="weapon" guid="019ed39c-6321-7c51-9691-f59b441b0bec">Silence</entity> intended to be through him and past him before the body finished falling. He brought <entity repo="weapon" guid="cd8ce222-de5f-44c4-b6f6-5c18721c1050">the blade</entity> across his body and settled. His right foot slid back a quarter step into the line <entity repo="character" guid="01a02d38-185c-7752-b83e-baa921571078">Seito</entity> had drilled into him — <entity repo="character" guid="01a02d38-185c-7752-b83e-baa921571078">Seito</entity>, the only teacher the neuretics had left him a full record of, who'd worked him for nine years before letting him take jobs alone. Weight into his hips. Knees soft. The blade came to chest height, edge aligned with the centerline of his body, the wrap cord taking his sweat without slip. His shoulders dropped. His breath came down.

The stance was the stance. From here he could move in any direction. From here every muscle was already loaded. From here <entity repo="weapon" guid="cd8ce222-de5f-44c4-b6f6-5c18721c1050">the blade</entity> could reach any throat in the room without traveling more than eight inches. The one afternoon the foot-line had been corrected for the last time, he couldn't find in memory. The neuretics kept that kind of thing as a result, not a moment. At some point that had stopped bothering him, and he couldn't find that moment either.

He held <entity repo="weapon" guid="019ed39c-6321-7c51-9691-f59b441b0bec">Silence</entity> in front of him like a question.

No one moved.

<entity repo="weapon" guid="4ab24f74-61d4-4f45-b326-7c6b98c96279">Cacophony</entity> stayed on his hip.

The room could be crossed. He'd settled that before his boot came through the door — twenty-some feet of dock floor, six bodies, a card table, and a route between them the array had drawn in the half-second before anyone thought to stand. The gun was for plans that failed. He hadn't failed to plan.

<entity repo="weapon" guid="019ed39c-6321-7c51-9691-f59b441b0bec">Silence</entity> moved. What the room heard was almost nothing: a chair going over, a bottle ringing on the concrete, the wet exhale of men who understood the weather was already on top of them. <entity repo="weapon" guid="019ed39c-6321-7c51-9691-f59b441b0bec">Silence</entity> found a shoulder tendon — the exact one a man's swing had been counting on — and the arm finished its arc anyway, half a second of momentum running on nothing but memory. The loudest sound on the dock was chrome hitting the floor. The blood made no sound at all. It simply went where the cuts sent it, and every cut had been told where to stop.

The boy threw first, because the boy had thrown first his whole short career. The haymaker came up out of the chair with his hips and his heart behind it, the knuckle plates firing on the upswing so the fist came round trailing sparks like a grinder kissing steel. It was a proven punch. It had ended arguments. It had broken jaws — older jaws, slower jaws, jaws on men who'd asked for one more week and stood there hoping while it wound up. Every jaw it broke taught the boy the same wrong lesson: that the punch worked.

The punch worked on people who couldn't afford to move. A haymaker is a power move, but it is also a promise: I am going to hit you from here, and I cannot change my mind. The whole line from hip to knuckle was already committed, the boy's center of gravity already past the point of correction. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> had already moved. He stepped inside the arc — not away from it, inside it, into the dead space where a haymaker is just a man falling in a circle — set his palm against the boy's shoulder blade as the weight went past, and helped. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> waited. He had time to stand in the blood and wait for her to make a choice.

He stood. He needed the girl to come to him on her own — no lunging, no grabbing, nothing that would send her bolting back into the dark where he couldn't follow. He walked toward the ventilation unit and stopped short of it. He did not go behind it. He stayed where she could see him — a tall, starved shape in the dock's bad light, carrying more of his own blood than anyone else's. He waited.

The pier smelled like rust and brine and the specific cold that comes off deep water at night. Behind the ventilation unit the breathing had stopped, gone to the absolute quiet wounded things make when they hope the predator loses interest. He gave her the silence back. He could stand like this for hours. His shoulder throbbed on its own slow rhythm, a thing he had long ago learned not to think about. None of it changed the fact of him being motionless, patient, and absolutely committed to not moving until she moved.

Then something moved, slow and low. A scrape of shoe sole on corrugated steel. A shape resolved itself out of the dark the way things do when they've been waiting for permission — not fast, not slow, just the breathing getting louder as it came. A face came out of the dark. Twelve, maybe thirteen. Her clothes were gray-zone reclaim, layers washed past any original color, and her hair was pulled back with something that might have been wire. She had her father's jaw and her mother's eyes. Her face was doing too many things at once, and none of them belonged on a child.

Her father's jaw. These three teeth. One stood for the other now.

He crouched to her height, slow, and opened his left hand between them. The three teeth lay in his palm, still wet, still catching what little light reached the dock floor.

She had to get them somewhere safe before the man who'd worn them woke and demanded them back. Her eyes tracked to his hand and stayed there. Her jaw tightened. He opened his fingers wider, and the teeth fell into her cupped palms.

She shrieked — high and thin. The sound bounced off the hard surfaces of the dock and came back wrong, doubled, off the mooring lines and the pier supports and the perimeter lights cycling through their sweep. But she did not drop them. Her fingers closed. She looked at her closed hands.

Then she bowed — a full-body jerk of terror and something close to thanks, though it wasn't quite thanks — and she was gone, swallowed by the dark past the door.

He cleaned <entity repo="weapon" guid="cd8ce222-de5f-44c4-b6f6-5c18721c1050">the blade</entity> again anyway — oil, paper, the whole sequence. On the second pass the paper slid two inches off the flat and he had to catch it. The edge pulled wrong in his grip. It took him half a second to understand the problem wasn't <entity repo="weapon" guid="cd8ce222-de5f-44c4-b6f6-5c18721c1050">the blade</entity>. It was his hand.

The tremor started on the right. It crossed to the left. For a moment both hands shook. This was the crash — thousands of calories spent in twenty seconds, and now the body was collecting the bill. His stomach was a closed fist. He needed protein and carbohydrate. Something hot in a bowl. Something that asked nothing of him. He needed to sit somewhere that smelled like anything other than this.

He set <entity repo="weapon" guid="cd8ce222-de5f-44c4-b6f6-5c18721c1050">the blade</entity> down before it dropped itself. Fine. He'd find the noodle place two streets over, take the corner table, and put something in his gut before it decided things for him.

The bike was where he'd left it, chained to a drainage pipe two docks down. Eleven years old, the paint faded to the color of old rust, and he'd kept it that way on purpose — nothing about it drew attention, nothing about it suggested the man who rode it had done anything at all. He got the lock open on the third try — his fingers still weren't his own — and swung the chain free.

He needed to be off the pier before the port authority's sweep started, and he needed the plate swapped before he crossed into surveillance territory, and he needed both of those things to happen on a body that was currently negotiating with him about whether it would stand up straight.

The plate under the seat was Gray Zone standard — good enough for a dock crew's cameras, wrong for anything Axiom ran. He'd swap it two streets short of West Town, where the Tier read changed and the wrong plate turned a <entity repo="vocabulary" guid="019d6143-aa8f-796a-8b70-7076ec482c7f">clean exit</entity> into a flagged one. The spare was keyed to a shell corp that had ceased existing three years back; the fasteners were already stripped from the last dozen swaps, so it would sit loose enough to rattle if he hit the right frequency, tight enough to pass a casual scan. Not here. Here the plate stayed.

He got the bike upright. His knee didn't want the weight and took it anyway.

The engine caught on the second try — a grinding hesitation before the magnetic coupling found itself, then the low throb settling into his sternum. He throttled low, easing off the dock's corrugated steel and onto the access ramp, past a checkpoint light that had been dead for longer than he'd been running this route. Nobody manned it. Nobody had in years. That was <entity repo="place" guid="019d6143-a94e-7740-8aa9-4b82bbd9a223">the Gray Zone</entity>'s whole arrangement with itself: watch where it's profitable, and let the rest go dark.

He rode north along the seawall access road, the old Barrier looming to his right, sixty feet of concrete and carbon composite that had never once been asked to hold back what it was built for. <entity repo="motif" guid="019d6143-a8e2-727a-be75-32648e8aaa47">Rain</entity> hadn't started yet but the air had that pressure to it, the smell of ozone and standing water that meant it would — the atmospheric processors overhead were running a redistribution cycle, pulling the weather north toward the Axiom sectors and pushing whatever it didn't want down onto the tiers where nobody with money lived.

Carver's proof rode zipped in his inside pocket, against his ribs, next to the rig. Midnight was the drop window and midnight wasn't close yet, but a job wasn't closed until the buyer had it in hand, and <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> had learned a long time ago not to call something finished before it was.

His stomach folded on itself again, a specific hollow ache that had nothing to do with the blood loss and everything to do with twenty seconds of maximum output and nothing since. He was hungry in the animal way, the way that made him think about food and not want, exactly, but need — protein, salt, something with weight to it.

He was tired in the way that sat behind the eyes.

He was alive, and the bike knew the road to Chen's without him steering it, which was good, because for the first six blocks he mostly just held on.

He stopped at a light outside a bar with no name. Its hood lamp burned the same tired orange as every other hood lamp, that municipal orange the arcologies had stopped using decades ago and the flats had never been able to afford to replace. Two operators stood arguing the way operators argue — that specific posture of people whose job was to move through a space and leave it altered — loud enough that the array pulled the thread off the open band on its own.

One of them had a relay up. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> could see the glow on his face from across the intersection.

"No broker stamp," the man kept saying, tilting the relay at the other one. "No operator attachment. The thing posted itself. You understand what I'm telling you?"

"Self-posted?" The other one laughed at him for spooking at a clean contract. "That doesn't happen. Somebody's running the relay dark to hide the chain."

"Posted at 22:47. No chain. No attribution. Just the work order and the fee. In Φ, up front." The first man's voice climbed. "You take a job with Φ up front, you're taking it from someone. There's always someone. This one there's no someone."

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> noticed the shape of it, the way he noticed running lights and bad light at <entity repo="place" guid="019fbde4-f17d-7bfa-9548-2f248f4e8362">Cermak</entity> and Loomis — the seam in the ordinary that the neuretics registered before the conscious mind caught up. A job from nowhere. No operator listed on the board. No broker. No shell that resolved to a face. He had heard the same shape twice before. He had not yet decided it was a shape.

The other one had stopped laughing.

Tonight he wanted one thing and one thing only: to get across town, drop the fare, and log off clean without another self-posting job snagging his relay. Keep his head down. Keep the band quiet. The body was still negotiating with him — the hands not quite steady, the stomach a closed fist — and it did not need a mystery to work on.

The light changed. Before he pulled away, he looked once more at the relay's open band. The job was still there — a rate, a task, and no one behind them. He closed it without marking it. He rode on.

title: Something Fixed
text:
He knocked in the morning, and <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> opened the door already talking.

"Forearm first, then the array. Then you tell me why your calibration log has a gap in it shaped like a man who doesn't want to explain something." She had a soldering iron in one hand, yesterday's hair, and the sharp focus of someone who'd been up a while. "Sit. Not there. There. The light's honest there."

The shoulder she'd already dealt with at the door - two words, "through, clean," and enough pressure-packed gauze to hold it while she worked her way down the rest of him. Arguing with her about triage order had never once worked.

Across the hall was four steps. Somewhere in there the steps had stopped being a trip and become a place he wanted to go.

She took the field dressing off his forearm the way she took everything off him — without ceremony, telling him where her hands were before he felt them. "Three inches. Not to the bone, but you let someone do this." Not a question. She threaded the suture. The needle met the wound edge; the tissue had already started to close, and it pushed back, fine and particular, the body working the problem on its own. She moved through it clean. She drew the thread and set the knot with both thumbs. The suture pulled snug at exactly the tension the wound needed. "You let him, because not letting him would have cost more. And you decide that in a quarter-second and never explain yourself, which is the single most annoying thing about you, and I've made a list." She tore a strip of biotape and laid it down slow. "Eat the egg. It's on the counter. Don't tell me you're not hungry. Your body's burning a thousand calories an hour fixing what you spent last night, and one bowl at the noodle place doesn't cover it, because Carver paid you in whole Qs and you wouldn't break one for a second bowl. Eat the egg, <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>."

He ate the egg.

Morning light came through her east window at a low angle, honest and a little cold. The overnight processors had left condensation on the glass. He'd been here enough mornings to know the light by how it felt, not where it came from.

The array took longer. She set the contacts at the base of his skull, ran the calibration, and went very quiet. That was how he knew she'd found the brownout before she said it. "It double-printed. The duel's last cut - you went a beat blind and it came back wrong at the edges." She scrolled. On her console the waveform of his array sang its normal song, the whole lattice bright and steady. Underneath it, barely visible, rode something else — a frequency that didn't belong, present and not quite present, a stowaway on the baseline. She adjusted the sweep, ran it again, watched it hold. "And there's the harmonic again. Low, steady, under everything. Older than any spec I have for your hardware - older than the hardware itself. The integration's clean, that's the part I hate. Your hardware treats it like it belongs. I've flagged it three times. It never changes and it never goes away and I can't find its source, and I hate that, professionally, more than I can tell you."

He'd felt it once or twice himself. Not heard it - felt it, the way you notice a refrigerator only when it stops. There was a version of this morning where he told her that. But a quieter, older thing in him — the same thing that had kept him alive eleven years — did not want to know what she'd find at the bottom of it. He let the urge pass.

"Some facility gear never came with specs," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> said. It was true. It was not an answer, and she let it not be one.

She unclipped the contacts. Pressed two fingers flat between his shoulder blades for half a second. Then it was gone, and she was a professional again. "You're recalibrated. You're sutured. You owe me forty for the array and you'll pay it exact, because you're you. And don't think the egg was free either. It's coming out of your dignity."

He pulled the credstick, transferred the forty, set it on the table beside the egg bowl. The transaction cleared and the stick was just a stick again. She didn't look at it. She never did; the look would have been an accusation that she trusted him to short her, and she didn't waste that on him.

She packed the tools into the bag. At the door she paused, not quite looking at him, the way she did when she'd already said the real thing with her hands. He wasn't sure when it had changed from her knowing him to her keeping track of him.

After she left, he read the relay. There was a secondary bounce he hadn't set - eight days old, <entity repo="character" guid="05fbd9d0-c6d5-4731-8e48-f1a4c59e8783">Sift</entity> shell, timestamped three hours before the <entity repo="place" guid="019ee6ce-9455-7d19-8916-e2d002eb8e89">Northpoint</entity> job. He saw it. The device was already back on the table, set down by a hand that had moved while he was still reading. He closed it.

title: The Log
text:
The crew's morning report came through the slot at 08:40, five different hands on one sheet, the way it always came now.

06:12 — TARGET (KYLE) EXITED. LIMP, LEFT SIDE, MINOR. RODE NORTH.
06:55 — PIGEON ON THE RAIL AGAIN. SAME PIGEON. WE HAVE NAMED IT. ITS NAME IS PROBLEM.
07:30 — A MAN PHOTOGRAPHED THE BUILDING FROM THE NOODLE SIDE. NOT A COP. TOO CLEAN.
07:31 — DENTS SAYS TOO CLEAN MEANS CORPO. RAFF SAYS TOO CLEAN MEANS NEW. WE PUT IT TO A VOTE.
07:34 — IT WAS A TIE. THIS LOG IS HONEST.

<entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-04fb-7227-94d9-6b4d889ce52b">Boost</entity> had signed it at the bottom the way she signed everything — a single capital B with a flourish she'd been refining for weeks. Under it: the clean man came back twice. that's a subscription, not a look. — B.

The kid was fourteen, and she was right. A man who came back twice on a schedule wasn't watching <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>. He was keeping a file on him. That meant someone was paying to keep the file current. And a file someone paid for was a file someone could buy — and there was exactly one counter in the city where a thing like that got sold honestly.

He turned the sheet over, looking for the second half of <entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-04fb-7227-94d9-6b4d889ce52b">Boost</entity>'s note — the part where she told him *who* the clean man's subscription belonged to, because <entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-04fb-7227-94d9-6b4d889ce52b">Boost</entity> never left a thread that short. The back was blank. Then he saw it, small, in the corner where the fold had hidden it: *07:41 — he saw me seeing him. smiled. left a card in our slot.* Taped beneath the words was the card itself. No name. No number. Cream stock, the kind that cost money to print, and a hand-inked line pressed into it: *We already bought the file. Come ask what it says.*

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> sat with that for the length of three breaths. Not a threat. Not quite a promise. A statement of fact left by someone who'd known <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> would read it alone, in a room with the door shut, and would understand it without anyone saying the rest out loud. The crew hadn't found a lead this morning. They'd been handed a hook, and they'd bitten before he ever read the log — which meant whoever wanted him at that counter had known he'd come to it, and had gotten there first. The clean man hadn't come inside. Hadn't waited. He'd walked <entity repo="place" guid="381616e9-d6a3-595d-e865-ce4b15d9310e">The Pivot</entity> twice on a schedule and left, spine out, without a second look. That was the whole message. That was the shape of someone who understood exactly how much to leave and how much to keep.

"Don't," said <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> from his doorway, his Φ40 in her hand. She'd come to collect and read his face instead. "You're going to go see the dead-tech man?"

"<entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-1ab1-78dc-bbb2-58870428613d">Vey</entity> keeps better records than the city does. He hears about a file before it's sold — he's the counter it gets sold across."

"<entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-1ab1-78dc-bbb2-58870428613d">Vey</entity> keeps records the city can't reach, which is a different and worse sentence." She held out the credstick. "Eat something at the actual market on the way. A thing with vegetables in it. I'll know."

title: Rotterdam
text:
<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> was waiting on the platform at Dock 14 with a coffee she did not offer him and a smart-dust reader she did.

"They tagged you," she said. "Last night, the noodle side. A microgram of marker dust on your right shoulder — the clean man, has to be. It's been singing your position to a collector on a four-hour clock since 06:00." She turned him toward the platform light, fingers tracing the seam where his shirt met his neck — the reading touch, not the medical one, the way she'd learned to scan a surface without instruments. There it was: iridescent, barely in the weave, the kind of thing that registered only when you knew what to look for. Tracer-grade. <entity repo="material" guid="f0bf1d78-f851-37f3-0c42-9ca8443b8890">Ferrocement</entity> compound, the kind that moved through the <entity repo="corponation" guid="0d831459-182f-4efc-9920-bdf9e032c61d">Pulse</entity> network and reported back. She wasn't angry. She was delighted, the way she got when a problem turned out to be solvable and rude. "I could pull it. But pulling it tells them you found it, and then they get clever, and clever's expensive."

"Or," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> said.

"Or," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> agreed. They both looked at the 14:17 <entity repo="corponation" guid="0d831459-182f-4efc-9920-bdf9e032c61d">Pulse</entity> freight slug standing on the rail, sealed and humming, forty-three minutes from <entity repo="place" guid="01a06ee1-ed6c-7a54-97a5-56afca1f1f19">Rotterdam</entity> at Mach six. Agricultural substrate, bulk feed under the manifest window. "Marker dies in the substrate noise inside six hours," she said, half to herself. "But it reaches <entity repo="place" guid="01a06ee1-ed6c-7a54-97a5-56afca1f1f19">Rotterdam</entity> first. Whoever's buying the file gets a false endpoint. No waste."

He walked past the slug close enough to brush it and let the marker dust find a new home — a pod bound under the North Atlantic, where it would go on reporting his position, with great confidence, from the wrong continent. He moved like nothing had changed, because that was the trick: not the transfer, the walk after it. He did not check his shoulder. He did not look back at the slug.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> finally handed him the coffee. "Somebody in an office files that you're in <entity repo="place" guid="01a06ee1-ed6c-7a54-97a5-56afca1f1f19">Rotterdam</entity>. Somebody above them believes it, because it's on the system." She watched the slug go. "Everybody trusts the paper. <entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-1ab1-78dc-bbb2-58870428613d">Vey</entity>'s the only one who charges for the truth."

"<entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-1ab1-78dc-bbb2-58870428613d">Vey</entity> says the truth's an object."

"<entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-1ab1-78dc-bbb2-58870428613d">Vey</entity> would." She drank. "Did you eat?"

"There were vegetables," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> said, which was true and was not an answer, and she let it not be one. They walked back up into the city a half-step apart, the way they always did — the pod reporting his ghost under the Atlantic, <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> walking where she could see him without turning her head.
